...Teeth ‘n’ Smiles now functions as a history play, giving context to the state we are in.
In the end, Maggie’s screams ring out around the cloisters, the dreaming spires where acid dreams go to die.

It’s a good cast, too - notably Michael Fox as Maggie’s intellectual old flame (possibly Hare’s self-portrait), Roman Asde as the bumbling, smitten student, and Phil Daniels, a total treat as the cynical old band manager. This is sharp, funny, smile-inducing pleasure for rock-loving graduates of a certain vintage.

Originally starring Helen Mirren, the cue for revival is that the band’s lead singer Maggie, a Johnny Walker-pickled dipsomaniac, is played by the singer-songwriter Rebecca Lucy Taylor (also known as Self Esteem). The fictional band she fronts is a fusion of Led Zeppelin and Def Leppard.
His verdict: “thoroughly entertaining”, and sure to “enjoy a long and sold-out run at the beautiful Savoy Theatre.”
The play falls apart in the second act as Maggie gets increasingly depressed and Saraffian delivers a series of meandering speeches.
There's fun to be had in Daniel Raggett's production, stripping away distraction and funnelling all attention onto Maggie's slow-motion implosion.
Beyond that, this David Hare revival is toothless.
Some good things, some bad things in David Hare's old play

Among the supporting cast, there is excellent work. Phil Daniels is a standout as Sarrafian, grounding the production with a seasoned, understated performance. Michael Fox is equally strong, bringing nuance to Arthur and offering one of the evening’s most engaging character arcs.
But ultimately too many of the narrative arcs, fights and breakdowns feel contrived and surface-level.

There appears to be no character depth or development, no serious issues explored and little insight into a fragment of a drunken subculture that has no sense of the world in which it is supposed to exist.
